title: The Supreme Court Is Weeks Away from Ruling on Birthright Citizenship. Indian Visa Holders Have the Most at Stake.
excerpt: Trump became the first sitting president to attend oral arguments in April. Six justices pushed back. The ruling, expected by late June, could redefine who counts as American-born.
body:
Sometime in the next few weeks, the United States Supreme Court will hand down a ruling that could alter the legal status of thousands of children born to Indian parents on American soil. The case — *Trump v. Barbara* — challenges a constitutional guarantee that has been settled law for 128 years.

At its centre is Executive Order 14160, signed by President Donald Trump on his first day back in office in January 2025. The order directs federal agencies to deny citizenship documents to children born in the United States whose parents are on temporary visas — including H-1B, F-1, L-1, and H-4 holders — or are undocumented. Every lower court that has reviewed the order has blocked it as unconstitutional.

But the administration appealed, and the Supreme Court heard oral arguments on April 1. Trump attended in person, becoming the first sitting president in American history to sit in on a Supreme Court argument. He watched from the front row for 90 minutes.

## What the Justices Signalled

The arguments did not go well for the government. Six of the nine justices — including two Trump appointees — appeared sceptical of the administration's reading of the Fourteenth Amendment, which states that "all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens."

The government argued that children of temporary visa holders are not fully "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States because their parents owe allegiance to another country. Chief Justice John Roberts pushed back directly, telling the administration's lawyer: "It is a new world, but it is the same Constitution."

The government declined to ask the court to overturn *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, the 1898 precedent that established birthright citizenship for children of foreign nationals born on U.S. soil. That concession narrowed its legal path significantly.

Legal observers now expect the court to rule against the executive order, possibly by a lopsided margin. But the question of scope matters. A narrow ruling might leave room for Congress to legislate restrictions in the future. A broad affirmation of *Wong Kim Ark* would close that door.

## Why Indian Families Are Watching Closely

Indians are the largest group of H-1B visa holders in the United States, accounting for roughly 72 percent of approvals in recent years. Tens of thousands of Indian families on H-1B and H-4 visas have children born in America — children who, under current law, are citizens from birth.

If the court were to side with the administration — which most analysts consider unlikely — the consequences would be immediate and severe. Children could be denied passports, Social Security numbers, and access to Medicaid and CHIP benefits. A USCIS memo from July 2025 outlined a potential $1,600 "status verification" fee for newborns whose parents' immigration status is in question.

Even before the ruling, the executive order has created a chilling effect. Immigration lawyers report a surge in inquiries from Indian families seeking to understand their children's legal exposure. Some families have begun carrying birth certificates and legal documentation at all times — a precaution that would have seemed absurd a year ago.

## A Broader Pattern

The birthright case is one of several immigration-related decisions the court is expected to deliver before its term ends this month. A separate case involves the administration's effort to strip Temporary Protected Status from hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian immigrants — a case where the government's prospects appear stronger.

Taken together, the immigration docket reflects a court navigating the tension between executive ambition and constitutional limits. The arguments in the birthright case suggested that even a 6-3 conservative majority has boundaries — particularly when 128 years of precedent and the plain text of the Fourteenth Amendment point in the same direction.

For Indian Americans, the ruling will be more than a legal outcome. It will signal whether the country they have built lives in still considers their American-born children unambiguously American.

## What to Do Now

Immigration attorneys advise H-1B and H-4 families with U.S.-born children to keep certified copies of birth certificates readily accessible, maintain documentation of their own legal visa status, and consult a licensed immigration attorney if they receive any government communication questioning their child's citizenship. The current federal court injunction in *Barbara v. Trump* continues to protect all affected families while the Supreme Court deliberates.

The ruling is expected by late June or early July 2026.
